headline: What to Look for in Post-Remodel Interior Painting
articleBody: Interior painting is usually the final trade in a remodel, but its quality depends heavily on surface preparation, dust control, and curing conditions. The EPA’s lead-safe renovation guidance is particularly relevant in older Los Angeles homes because disturbing paint in pre-1978 properties can create lead hazard concerns. Even without lead issues, a repaint after renovation should follow patching, sanding, priming, and moisture correction so that new finishes do not fail early. Buyers should ask whether the contractor or painter includes caulking, drywall repair, stain blocking, and color sampling, because “paint only” bids can omit the work that makes the finish look even. In humid rooms such as bathrooms and laundry areas, the painter should specify coatings suitable for moisture exposure and cleanability. Good interior painting services also account for schedule coordination with flooring, cabinetry, and trim installation, because paint damage from later trades is common. Homeowners should compare the prep scope more than the number of coats, since adhesion and appearance depend on substrate quality. The contractor should also explain whether low-VOC products are available and whether odor-sensitive occupancy needs will affect product selection. After a renovation, painting is not just decorative; it is also a protective layer that can reveal or hide workmanship quality in earlier trades, which is why careful specification matters.
